description: We are D-Verse, a younger brother and older sister team passionate about science, technology, and space. We love exploring new ideas, learning from each other, and turning our curiosity into real projects. We're excited to meet creative and curious people who enjoy building things together. We'd especially love to connect with people interested in programming, AI, engineering, design, or scientific research.
summary:
We built ALAZ because fire is one of the biggest risks on any spacecraft, and the flight data that could help is hard to use. Without gravity a flame turns into a ball, the ventilation keeps it alive, and some materials keep burning at oxygen levels that would put them out on Earth. NASA studied this in 17 combustion experiments on the ISS. The results are public, but the 2,862 test records sit in separate tables with different units and different levels of detail.

ALAZ puts all of it in one place. You can open any experiment, compare two or three of them, or describe your own cabin and see whether NASA has ever tested those conditions. Our own AI model answers questions from the data and always says where the answer came from. Everything runs in the browser, for free.

One thing ALAZ makes obvious: solids have only been burned in orbit up to 22.2% oxygen, but Moon habitats are planned at 30% or more. Nobody has flight data for that range yet.
details:
What it does

ALAZ is for people who need to know what NASA's flight data says about fire under a given set of conditions: mission planners, fire safety engineers, researchers, and students who are just getting into the topic. It covers 17 combustion investigations from NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) archive. Some burn solid materials (BASS, BASS-II, Saffire), some study gas flames (the ACME series, SPICE, SLICE), some burn single fuel droplets (FLEX, FLEX-2, CFI), and three look at smoke (SAME, SAME-R, DAFT).

How it works

We went through the PSI tables and documents for each investigation and rewrote 2,862 test records into the same format, so fuel, oxygen, pressure, airflow, gravity, sensors and results can finally be compared. Every value keeps a link back to where it came from.

The site has five pages. Learn explains the basic physics. Catalog lists the experiments, opens a detailed panel for each one, and lets you compare up to three side by side. Simulation is where you enter your own oxygen level, pressure, airflow, gravity and material. ALAZ checks each of those against what was actually flown and gives Pass, Conditional or Fail. We want to be clear about Fail: it doesn't mean the material will burn. It means nobody has tested that condition in space, so there's no data to lean on. Tools ranks the experiments by how well they match a mission.

The AI model

The AI model behind ALAZ is built on NASA data. Its knowledge comes entirely from the 17 PSI investigations: every fact it can use was generated from the NASA dataset, and it has no other source. This is not the kind of chatbot people are familiar with. It is much more topic-focused and talks exclusively about these experiments. One model, trained on 702 example questions, works out what kind of question was asked. A second one, trained on 3,551 questions, handles questions inside the experiment panel. Then a concept engine picks out what the question is really about (oxygen, pressure, flame spread and so on) and builds the answer from the NASA facts. That is why every answer can point to a PSI record or a paper, and why it says so when a question goes beyond the data.

Why it matters

Checking whether a design has any flight data behind it used to mean digging through a lot of files. Now it takes a few seconds. The clearest example is oxygen: solids have been burned in orbit at no more than 22.2%, while Moon habitat plans use 30% or more. That 7.8-point range has never been tested in space, and ALAZ shows it on one screen. We think that's a good starting point for deciding what the next experiment should be. The platform is free, works offline, doesn't send anything anywhere, and is available in English and Turkish, so teachers can use it too.

Testing

We wrote a separate script that recalculated 78,336 simulation cases from scratch, and it matched every time. For the AI model, we wrote our test questions before writing the answer code, so we couldn't tune the answers to the test. It got 78 to 89 percent right on the first try, depending on the question set, and it turned down all 20 off-topic questions.

Tools

HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript. No framework, no server, no database. We trained the models in Python using only the standard library. All data is from NASA PSI.

Decisions we made

Some values simply aren't in PSI. For BASS and SPICE, for example, there are no numeric atmosphere values in the data files. In those cases we show what NASA's own documents say, mark it clearly, and leave it out of the calculations. We didn't fill any gaps with guesses. We also kept the whole thing simple on purpose, so it costs nothing to run and should still work years from now.

What it can't do yet

We haven't tested it with real users. There's no flight data for Moon or Mars gravity, so ALAZ can only show the limits there. And it's a guide, not a tool for certifying materials.

AI tools

We used an AI assistant (Claude) to help resolve errors in our code and to assist with translating text into English. The data belongs to NASA, and we personally verified the results ourselves.
